explanations.explanation: Eat is right, baker. Mark says the crowd gathered so that Jesus and His disciples "could not even eat." When I get that busy, it's because a batch is burning, and even then I grab a cookie. I think that's a LOT of people.

Sleep is a fair guess, since busy days make everybody tired. But the text says the crowd kept Jesus and His disciples from something else: they "could not even eat." Sleep doesn't come up in these verses. That's the one that went missing from the table.
Leave makes sense if you picture a packed house. But the text never says they were stuck inside. It says they "could not even eat." So the problem was a meal that never got to happen, friend.

His family, that's right. Mark 3:21 says that when His family heard about this, they went out to take custody of Him. The text tells us what they said, but it doesn't tell us why they said it, so I won't guess. I'll just say it's a tough moment.

The disciples were right there with Jesus, so it's an easy one to grab. But verse 20 says the crowd kept "He and His disciples" from eating. They were in the house with Him. The ones who went out to take custody of Him were His family (Mark 3:21).

The Pharisees show up a lot in the Gospels, so I get the pick. They aren't in this part of the story, though. The people who came down from Jerusalem here are scribes (Mark 3:22), and they're doing something different. The ones taking custody are His family (Mark 3:21).

True. Mark 3:21 says His family went out to take custody of Him, "saying, 'He is out of His mind.'" That's a hard thing to hear about Jesus from the people closest to Him. I think this one stings a little.

It's the other way around. Mark 3:21 says His family went out to take custody of Him, "saying, 'He is out of His mind.'" So the words really were said. I think it's a heavy line, and the passage doesn't hide it.

The prince of the demons, you got it. The scribes said, "By the prince of the demons He drives out demons" (Mark 3:22). They also said He was possessed by Beelzebul. That's quite a claim, and Jesus is about to answer it.

Elijah was a prophet of Israel, so I see where you were going. But the scribes didn't name him at all. They said, "By the prince of the demons He drives out demons" (Mark 3:22). Elijah isn't in this story.
The high priest is a big name, but he isn't part of this accusation. The scribes from Jerusalem said, "By the prince of the demons He drives out demons" (Mark 3:22). That's the power they pointed to.
Jesus says the opposite. Mark 3:24 says, "If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand." He doesn't add any exception for a strong one. Divided means it can't stand, however big it is.

False is right. Jesus says, "If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand" (Mark 3:24). Nothing in that line about being strong enough. When I try to bake with two cooks pulling the oven in opposite directions, nobody wins.

End is right, baker. Jesus says, "And if Satan is divided and rises against himself, he cannot stand; his end has come" (Mark 3:26). He's answering the scribes' idea with a plain picture. A divided side doesn't last.

Reward sounds like the kind of word that could fit a sentence like this. But Jesus says, "he cannot stand; his end has come" (Mark 3:26). A side divided against itself doesn't come out ahead. It comes to its end.
Victory would be a big surprise here, friend. Jesus actually says the opposite: "he cannot stand; his end has come" (Mark 3:26). Being divided against yourself isn't a winning plan. The word is end.

Ties up the strong man, yes. Jesus says no one can enter a strong man's house to steal his possessions "unless he first ties up the strong man" (Mark 3:27). The order matters: tie him up first, then the house. The text doesn't say more than that.

explanations.answer: Waits for the strong man to leave
explanations.explanation: Waiting for him to leave is a sneaky plan, and I respect the thinking. But Jesus doesn't mention it. He says no one can steal from the house "unless he first ties up the strong man" (Mark 3:27). The strong man gets dealt with first.

explanations.answer: Pays off the strong man's servants
explanations.explanation: Paying off servants is a whole heist movie, baker. Jesus doesn't go there. He says the thief has to "first tie up the strong man" (Mark 3:27). No servants and no payments in that picture.

True. Jesus says no one can steal from the house unless he first ties up the strong man, and then adds, "Then he can plunder his house" (Mark 3:27). Tie him up first, and then the house. It's a short picture with a clear order.
Jesus actually says it happens. After the strong man is tied up, He says, "Then he can plunder his house" (Mark 3:27). So the tying up comes first, and then the plundering. That's the order He gives.

The Holy Spirit is right. Jesus says, "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin" (Mark 3:29). That's a serious line, and I won't joke about it. Mark tells us in verse 30 what was being said when Jesus spoke it.

The prophets are respected all over the Bible, so it's an easy guess. But Jesus doesn't name them here. He says it's "whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit" who "will never be forgiven" (Mark 3:29). That's a heavy verse, so it's worth getting the name right.

Angels are a fair guess, friend, but they aren't in this verse. Jesus says, "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven" (Mark 3:29). The name He gives is the Holy Spirit. It's a heavy verse, so I want it exact.

True. Jesus says whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit "will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin" (Mark 3:29). It follows His line that the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies (Mark 3:28). It's a serious part of the passage, and Mark ties it to what was being said in verse 30.

Jesus really does say it. Mark 3:29 reads, "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin." It's a heavy line. Mark explains right after that Jesus said this because they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit" (Mark 3:30).

He has an unclean spirit, yes. Mark 3:30 says, "Jesus made this statement because they were saying, 'He has an unclean spirit.'" The writer gives us the reason outright, so we don't have to guess. Good reading, baker.

The Sabbath did come up with Jesus earlier in Mark, so I see why that popped up. But here, Mark gives a different reason. "Jesus made this statement because they were saying, 'He has an unclean spirit'" (Mark 3:30). That's the charge in this scene.
Speaking against Moses is a serious charge, but it's not in this passage. Mark 3:30 says Jesus spoke "because they were saying, 'He has an unclean spirit.'" That's the one the writer names.

explanations.answer: He asks who His mother and brothers are
explanations.explanation: He asks a question, that's right. Jesus replies, "Who are My mother and My brothers?" (Mark 3:33). He doesn't answer right away, and I think that pause got the whole room's attention. Then He looks at the people around Him.

explanations.answer: He tells them to wait outside
explanations.explanation: Telling them to wait is a normal thing to say. But Mark doesn't record Jesus saying that. He replies with a question: "Who are My mother and My brothers?" (Mark 3:33). The text moves right to what He says next.

explanations.answer: He sends the crowd back home
explanations.explanation: Sending everybody home would have cleared the room fast. But the text doesn't say He did it. The crowd stays seated around Him, and He says, "Who are My mother and My brothers?" (Mark 3:33). Then He looks at them.

Jesus says the opposite, baker. Looking at those seated around Him, He says, "Here are My mother and My brothers!" (Mark 3:34). He calls them family, not just followers. That's a big word to give anybody.

False is right. Jesus looks at those seated in a circle around Him and says, "Here are My mother and My brothers!" (Mark 3:34). He doesn't stop at followers. He calls them family, and that's a warm thing to hear.

explanations.answer: Whoever does the will of God
explanations.explanation: Whoever does the will of God, you've got it. Jesus says, "For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother" (Mark 3:35). That's the door He opens to anybody. I'd have taken that welcome back in the drawer, friend.

explanations.answer: Whoever is born into His family
explanations.explanation: Being born into the family sounds like the natural answer, and His mother and brothers were standing outside. But Jesus doesn't point to birth. He says, "whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother" (Mark 3:35). The line is about doing God's will.

explanations.answer: Whoever comes from the land of Israel
explanations.explanation: Where you're from is a normal way to measure family, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says, "whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother" (Mark 3:35). Nothing about a homeland in that line, baker.
